title.en: Discrete Mathematics and Logic for Computing

tagline: REPLACE: one line under the title: what participants can do after the course
description: Participants practise the discrete mathematics and proof that computing degrees assume: sets, relations, logic, proof, counting and graphs. Code tests each claim on generated cases before it is proved, so the gap between testing and proof is visible. Labs link relations to joins, logic to rule checking, counting to collision and re-identification risk, and graphs to pipeline dependencies. Algorithms on graphs follow in FND-PRG-103.
audience: Beginners. Career changers and non-computing graduates closing bridging gaps before advanced study, and computing graduates refreshing the mathematics behind models; a placement test lets participants skip any course whose content they already command.
prerequisites: Writes short Python programs with lists, loops, functions and recursion (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)

outcomes.text: Identify whether a relation is a function, an equivalence or an order, and which properties it has, given twelve relations from data and software
outcomes.evidence: supervised AI-off test, at least 70% correct

outcomes.text: Distinguish valid from invalid arguments and translate plain-language rules into propositional and predicate logic, given five access and data-quality rules
outcomes.evidence: rules checked by truth table or solver, four of five correct

outcomes.text: Describe direct, contradiction and induction proofs and identify the gap in a flawed proof, given six short proofs, two with planted errors
outcomes.evidence: marked answers in the supervised test

outcomes.text: Apply induction and loop invariants to prove simple claims about integers, sets and recursive code, given claims first tested in code
outcomes.evidence: rubric-marked proofs, each with its test code

outcomes.text: Compute counts of arrangements, selections and collisions and verify them by enumeration, given hashing and record-linkage problems
outcomes.evidence: a notebook in which formula and brute-force counts agree

outcomes.text: Use a graph model of dependencies to find cycles and compute a topological order, given a pipeline graph with a planted cycle
outcomes.evidence: output naming the cycle and a valid order once it is removed
